title: A dog that barks, and still knows the animal sound

blocks.text: A subclass declared with `extends` inherits the superclass's non-private fields and methods, and adds its own. Constructors are **not** inherited: a subclass constructor hands its part of the state up with `super(...)`. An overriding method (marked `@Override`) runs in place of the superclass version, and `super.method()` still reaches the superclass version.
`Animals` holds two nested classes, taken from the lesson's own example. Write their bodies:

items: `Animal(String name)` stores the name in the `protected` field `name`; `getName()` returns it; `makeSound()` returns `"The animal makes a sound"`.
`Dog(String name)` is an `Animal`. Its constructor gives the name to `Animal`: `Dog` declares **no** field of its own.
`Dog.makeSound()` overrides the sound: `"<name> barks: Woof! Woof!"`.

blocks.text:
Animal pet = new Dog("Rex");
pet.makeSound()               -> "Rex barks: Woof! Woof!"
((Dog) pet).wagTail()         -> "Rex is wagging its tail"
new Dog("Rex").makeAnimalSound() -> "The animal makes a sound"
new Dog("Rex").getName()      -> "Rex"
new Animal("Generic").makeSound() -> "The animal makes a sound"

cases.says: A Dog seen through an Animal reference barks and wags its tail, and a plain Animal makes the generic sound.
makeAnimalSound() answers with Animal's version of the sound, not the dog's bark.
The dog's name is stored once, in Animal, so Animal's getName() returns it.

concepts: A subclass declared with extends inherits the superclass's non-private fields and methods and adds its own.
A subclass field with the superclass field's name hides it rather than replacing it, so state belongs in one place.
An overriding method keeps the name and parameters, is marked @Override, and runs in place of the superclass version.
Constructors are not inherited: a subclass constructor hands the superclass its state with super(...).
super.method() calls the superclass version of a method the subclass overrides.
